cases.question:
Use the Weave documentation at https://docs.wandb.ai/weave to answer this question:

How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?

candidate.answer:
They form one loop. **Tracing** records what your app or agent actually does. **Evaluations** measure quality against fixed test cases before you ship. **Signals** score live agent traffic automatically, so problems in production show up. Weave describes itself as an observability and evaluation platform that helps you understand what your AI application is doing, measure how well it performs, and improve it over time [S5].

- **Tracing (the foundation):** Traces capture each operation's inputs, outputs and structure as a *Call* (one recorded function or LLM call). They help you debug, evaluate and monitor LLM-powered code [S7]. There are two paths. Agent integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls and tool calls in the **Agents** view. LLM-application integrations capture individual Calls in the **Traces** view [S3].
- **Evaluations (testing before release):** An `Evaluation` object combines a dataset of examples with one or more scoring functions (*scorers*, which grade outputs). You run it against a model or function, and each run measures performance [S2]. This lets you track which model and prompt versions produced which results, compare evaluations across metrics, and spot regressions [S2, S6].
- **Signals (monitoring in production):** In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals can score response quality, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content, and they point you to the traces that need attention [S1]. A *rating* is a number from 0.0 to 1.0; a *tag* is a label such as "user-frustration". Both are applied to matching spans (parts of a trace), and a *turn* is one exchange between the user and the agent [S4].

**How they connect (my inference from the docs):** traced agent conversations are what Signals score. The traces that Signals flag show where quality is slipping, which can guide new test cases and re-running evaluations as you change prompts or models. Weave also says you can score production traffic with the same scorers you use in evaluation [S9].

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

> Learn about W&B Weave and how it helps you build, evaluate, and improve LLM applications

W\&B Weave is an observability and evaluation platform for building reliable agents and LLM applications. Weave helps you understand what your AI application is doing, measure how well it performs, and systematically improve it over time.

Building LLM applications is fundamentally different from traditional software development. LLM outputs are non-deterministic, making debugging harder. Quality is subjective and context-dependent. Small prompt changes can cause unexpected behavior changes. Traditional testing approaches fall short.

> Evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics with Weave Scorers

In Weave, Scorers evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics. They take the AI's output, analyze it, and return a dictionary of results. Scorers can use your input data as reference if needed and can also output extra information, such as explanations or reasoning from the evaluation.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

They form one loop. **Tracing** records what your app or agent actually does. **Evaluations** measure quality against fixed test cases before you ship. **Signals** score live agent traffic automatically, so problems in production show up. Weave describes itself as an observability and evaluation platform that helps you understand what your AI application is doing, measure how well it performs, and improve it over time [S5].

- **Tracing (the foundation):** Traces capture each operation's inputs, outputs and structure as a *Call* (one recorded function or LLM call). They help you debug, evaluate and monitor LLM-powered code [S7]. There are two paths. Agent integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls and tool calls in the **Agents** view. LLM-application integrations capture individual Calls in the **Traces** view [S3].
- **Evaluations (testing before release):** An `Evaluation` object combines a dataset of examples with one or more scoring functions (*scorers*, which grade outputs). You run it against a model or function, and each run measures performance [S2]. This lets you track which model and prompt versions produced which results, compare evaluations across metrics, and spot regressions [S2, S6].
- **Signals (monitoring in production):** In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals can score response quality, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content, and they point you to the traces that need attention [S1]. A *rating* is a number from 0.0 to 1.0; a *tag* is a label such as "user-frustration". Both are applied to matching spans (parts of a trace), and a *turn* is one exchange between the user and the agent [S4].

**How they connect (my inference from the docs):** turns in traced agent conversations are what Signals score. The traces that Signals flag show where quality is slipping, which can guide new test cases and re-running evaluations as you change prompts or models. # Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

> Learn about W&B Weave and how it helps you build, evaluate, and improve LLM applications

# Trace your code

> Instrument your running code so its execution appears as detailed traces in Weave.

This guide shows you how to instrument your application so that its execution appears as detailed traces in Weave. Traces help you debug, evaluate, and monitor LLM-powered code by capturing inputs, outputs, and the structure of each operation as a Call.

* Automatic tracking of LLM library calls.
* Tracking of custom functions with `weave.op`.
* Manual Call tracking using the API directly.

Choose the approach that fits how much control you need over what gets traced.

> Evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics with Weave Scorers

In Weave, Scorers evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics. They take the AI's output, analyze it, and return a dictionary of results. Scorers can use your input data as reference if needed and can also output extra information, such as explanations or reasoning from the evaluation.

This guide is for developers who want to measure the quality of their AI system's outputs. It explains how Scorers fit into Weave evaluations, how to build your own Scorers, how to apply Scorers to individual calls, and how to analyze the resulting scores.

1. **Function-based Scorers:** Python functions decorated with `@weave.op`.

## What gets traced

After you run an agent with the exporter enabled, Koog forwards traces to your Weave project. Koog's Weave exporter captures the same spans as Koog's general OTEL integration, including:

* Agent lifecycle events (start, stop, errors)
* LLM interactions (prompts, completions, token usage, latency)
* Tool and API calls (function calls and external requests)
* System context (model name, Koog version, environment metadata)

You can visualize these traces in the Weights & Biases UI to understand performance and quality. See [Weave's tracing overview](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for an introduction to capturing traces with Weave.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

cases.question: I'm using Python. What does weave.init do, and what project string should I pass?

candidate.answer:
`weave.init` turns on Weave tracking for your Python process and sends everything to one Weights & Biases project. Pass a string in the form `"team-name/project-name"`, or just `"project-name"` to use your default team [S1, S2].

**What it does**
- It starts Weave tracking for the project you name. After you call it, every call to a function decorated with `@weave.op` is logged to that project [S2].
- The setup applies to your whole program, so you don't need to keep the client it returns. It still returns a `WeaveClient` if you want one [S2].
- It also traces supported LLM libraries automatically. For example, once `weave.init` has run, all later OpenAI calls are traced, no matter when you imported `openai` [S3]. This behaviour is on by default and is controlled by the `implicitly_patch_integrations` setting [S2].
- Optional arguments let you set client settings, attach attributes to every trace, and change inputs or outputs before they're logged ("postprocessing") [S2].

**Which project string to pass**
- The first argument, `project_name`, is "the name of the Weights & Biases team and project to log to" [S2].
- `"my-team/my-project"`: logs to that specific team [S1].
- `"my-project"`: logs to your **default entity** (your default team or account). You can find or change it in your W&B user settings [S2, S3].

```python
import weave

# Log to a specific team
weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

# Or log to your default team/entity
# weave.init("[YOUR-PROJECT]")
```

Tip: write out the team name if you work in more than one team. That way traces don't end up in your default team by accident.

To enable Weave tracing for your Verdict pipelines, call `weave.init(project=...)` at the beginning of your script. Use the `project` argument to log to a specific Weights & Biases Team name with `team-name/project-name`, or pass `project-name` to log to your default team or entity.

Initialize weave tracking, logging to a wandb project.

Logging is initialized globally, so you do not need to keep a reference to the return value of init.

Following init, calls of weave.op decorated functions will be logged to the specified project.

**Args:**

NOTE: Client-level postprocessing runs after each op's own postprocessing. The order is always: 1. Op-specific postprocessing 2. Client-level postprocessing

* **`project_name`**: The name of the Weights & Biases team and project to log to. If you don't  specify a team, your default entity is used. * **`settings`**: Configuration for the Weave client generally. Can be a UserSettings instance or a dict  with any of the following keys (all optional). Default: `auto` - `use_server_cache` (bool): Enables local disk caching of server responses. - `server_cache_size_limit` (int): Cache size limit in bytes. Default: `~/.cache/wandb/weave-scorers` - `max_calls_queue_size` (int): Maximum queue size (0 = unbounded). Default: `100_000` - `retry_max_interval` (float): Maximum retry interval in seconds. ## Link to a conversation from your app

To deep-link from your own UI to a conversation in the Weave Agents view, build the URL from your entity, project, and the conversation id. `weave.init()` returns a client that carries `entity` and `project`, and `start_conversation` exposes `conversation_id`.

```python lines Python theme={"system"}
from weave.trace.urls import agent_conversation_path

client = weave.init(f"{TEAM}/{PROJECT}")

with weave.start_conversation(agent_name="research-bot") as conversation:
    # ... run turns ...
    url = agent_conversation_path(
        client.entity, client.project, conversation.conversation_id
    )
    print(f"View this conversation at {url}")
```

cases.question: I'm using Python. What does weave.init do, and what project string should I pass?

candidate.answer:
`weave.init` turns on Weave tracking for your Python process and sends everything to one Weights & Biases project. Pass a string in the form `"team-name/project-name"`, or just `"project-name"` to use your default team [S1, S2].

It also authenticates with Weights & Biases and configures the OpenTelemetry exporter that sends agent spans to the Agents view [S4].

**What it does**
- It starts Weave tracking for the project you name. After you call it, every call to a function decorated with `@weave.op` is logged to that project [S2].
- The setup applies to your whole program, so you don't need to keep the client it returns. It still returns a `WeaveClient` if you want one [S2].
- It also traces supported LLM libraries automatically. For example, once `weave.init` has run, all later OpenAI calls are traced, no matter when you imported `openai` [S3]. This behaviour is on by default and is controlled by the `implicitly_patch_integrations` setting [S2].
- Optional arguments let you set client settings, attach attributes to every trace, and change inputs or outputs before they're logged ("postprocessing") [S2].

**Which project string to pass**
- The first argument, `project_name`, is "the name of the Weights & Biases team and project to log to" [S2].
- `"my-team/my-project"`: logs to that specific team [S1].
- `"my-project"`: logs to your **default entity** (your default team or account). You can find or change it in your W&B user settings [S2, S3].

```python
import weave

# Log to a specific team
weave.init("[YOUR-TEAM]/[YOUR-PROJECT]")

# Or log to your default team/entity
# weave.init("[YOUR-PROJECT]")
```

Tip: write out the team name if you work in more than one team. That way traces don't end up in your default team by accident.

## Link to a conversation from your app

To deep-link from your own UI to a conversation in the Weave Agents view, build the URL from your entity, project, and the conversation id. `weave.init()` returns a client that carries `entity` and `project`, and `start_conversation` exposes `conversation_id`.

```python lines Python theme={"system"}
from weave.trace.urls import agent_conversation_path

client = weave.init(f"{TEAM}/{PROJECT}")

with weave.start_conversation(agent_name="research-bot") as conversation:
    # ... run turns ...
    url = agent_conversation_path(
        client.entity, client.project, conversation.conversation_id
    )
    print(f"View this conversation at {url}")
```

To attach custom metadata to your Verdict pipeline calls, use the [`weave.attributes`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/reference/python-sdk#function-attributes) context manager. import weave
